titre: Sandy Island, an Island on the Maps That Never Existed in the Water
accroche: Charted since 1876, Sandy Island is checked in 2012 by a research ship. There are only 1,300 meters of water at that spot.
contenu_vulgarise:
On Google Earth, in 2012, a large black patch marks an island in the Pacific between Australia and New Caledonia: Sandy Island, about 25 kilometers long. It also appears in scientific coastline databases used around the world. On November 22, 2012, a team of geologists from the University of Sydney aboard the research vessel Southern Surveyor, which left in October to study the tectonics of the Coral Sea, passes right over that spot. The navigation charts on board show a depth of 1,300 to 1,400 meters of water at the exact location of the island: far too deep for a sandbank ever to break the surface.

## The Mechanism

The origin of the error goes back to 1876, when the British whaler Velocity reports “breakers” and “sandy islets” at this spot in the Pacific, an observation repeated in an Australian maritime directory of 1879. The island then appears on a German chart of 1881, on a British Admiralty chart of 1895, then on charts from the British hydrographic office in 1908: never confirmed by any later passage, but never removed either. The French hydrographic service finally strikes it from its charts in 1974, after an aerial reconnaissance, and the Australian hydrographic service does the same in 1985, after a seabed survey. Two national navies had thus already settled the matter, some thirty years before Google Earth existed.

## The Shift

What makes the story interesting is not the initial 19th-century error (the breakers reported by a whaler could have been anything, a coral shoal breaking the surface or a trick of the swell) but its persistence after correction. The global coastline databases, later used to build digital maps and feed Google Earth, had copied old surveys without ever rechecking the area once the national hydrographic services had gone back over it. An island struck from the official charts in 1974 and 1985 thus kept existing in the major scientific datasets for nearly thirty years more.

The University of Sydney team published its discovery in 2013 in the journal Eos of the American Geophysical Union, under the mischievous title “Obituary: Sandy Island (1876-2012).” Google removed the island from its maps on November 26, 2012, four days after the expedition; the National Geographic Society did the same on November 29. The episode remains a textbook case of how a mapping error, once it has entered digital compilations, can survive indefinitely its own official correction: not through malice, but because copying existing data costs less than going back to check the field.

repere.texte: In 1974, then in 1985, the French and Australian hydrographic services remove Sandy Island from their official charts. It nonetheless keeps appearing in global coastline databases until November 2012.

carte.punch: In 2012, a research ship goes to check an island that has been on maps since 1876. There is nothing there but water.
carte.idee: Reported by a whaler in 1876, Sandy Island appears on maps for more than a century, removed from official surveys as early as 1974 but never from global coastline databases, until a research vessel finds, in 2012, that there are only 1,300 meters of water at that spot.

quiz.question: Why did Sandy Island keep appearing on global digital maps after its removal from the official French (1974) and Australian (1985) surveys?
choix: Because a sandbank re-formed at the same spot in the 1990s
Because the global coastline databases had copied old surveys without ever rechecking the area
Because the area lies in international waters and no country was responsible for updating it
Because satellites did not yet cover this part of the Pacific before the 2010s
quiz.explication: The French and Australian hydrographic services had struck the island from their own surveys as early as the 1970s-1980s, but the major coastline databases, the source of many digital maps including Google Earth, had simply copied old surveys without ever sending a ship back to check the area, until a scientific mission happened to pass through in 2012.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the initial report of Sandy Island, in 1876, come from?
choix: From a British whaler, the Velocity, which reports breakers and sandy islets
From a German chart drawn up by a Hamburg mapmaking firm
From an aerial survey carried out by the French hydrographic service
From an Australian scientific mission sent to study the tectonics of the Coral Sea
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The island is first reported in 1876 by the British whaler Velocity, which describes breakers and sandy islets, before being picked up in an Australian maritime directory in 1879.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long after the Southern Surveyor's passage does Google remove Sandy Island from its maps?
choix: The same day the ship passes
One year later, after verification by a second ship
Never: it is National Geographic that removes the island first, and Google never removes it afterward
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The team passes through on November 22, 2012 and finds the island absent; Google removes it from its maps on November 26, four days later, and National Geographic does the same on November 29.
